paper.title: RECENT ADVANCEMENTS IN SKELETON-BASED SIGN LANGUAGE RECOGNITION

description: A systematic review of skeleton-based sign recognition, focused mainly on isolated signs and model-family comparisons.
reason: Fails M2: Table 5 (p.13) compares three decoding settings from one CSLR study, not distinct studies. Table 3 and checks of the ambiguous cited methods do not establish a second qualifying CSLR study. M1 and M3 pass.

M1.reason: The abstract and methodology explicitly synthesize prior skeleton-based recognition research.

M2.reason: Only Takayama et al. (2022) is identified as a qualifying CSLR study. Table 5 compares settings within it; the ambiguous Buttar and Bencherif entries concern individual-sign classification. No comparison of two distinct CSLR studies was found.

M3.reason: The review covers body and hand pose/skeleton keypoints extracted from visual RGB data.

evidence.passage: Takayama and colleagues evaluate skeleton-based online continuous word recognition using monotonic attention on isolated-word and sentence videos. The abstract confirms this study's CSLR task; it does not establish a second distinct study in the review.

evidence.locator: PDF pp.1–4 (printed pp.184–187), Abstract, Introduction and Research methodology
evidence.passage: The title, authors and DOI match the candidate. The authors present a PRISMA-guided synthesis of 19 skeleton-based SLR studies; the introduction describes body and hand keypoints extracted from RGB video. This supports M1 and M3.

evidence.locator: PDF p.10 (printed p.193), Table 3 reference [6]; p.13 (printed p.196), Quantitative meta-analysis and Table 5; p.16, references
evidence.passage: Table 3 identifies Takayama et al. (2022), reference [6], as continuous/online recognition. The quantitative synthesis explicitly states that all continuous results come from one study. Table 5 compares its offline and two online decoding settings, each with k=1; these are not distinct prior studies.

evidence.locator: PDF pp.9–11 (printed pp.192–194), Table 3 references [8] and [11]; pp.6–8, dataset overview and Table 2; pp.12–15, taxonomy, synthesis and discussion
evidence.passage: The comparison labels Buttar et al. [8] and Bencherif et al. [11] as isolated SLR despite continuous-landmarks and mixed-sequence wording in their metrics. Dataset and discussion sections do not identify a second distinct CSLR study for comparison. A comparison of two qualifying CSLR studies was not found in the inspected full review.

evidence.locator: PDF p.5 (printed p.188), Results; p.1 Abstract; p.13 Table 5
evidence.passage: The Results paragraph states that three works address continuous recognition, but does not identify them. This conflicts with the abstract and explicit single-study synthesis. The unsupported aggregate count is recorded as a reporting inconsistency, not counted as three distinct studies.

evidence.locator: Primary cited paper: Abstract; Sections 3, 3.3.4 and 4.1; publisher text inspected via web search
evidence.passage: Despite continuous terminology, the methods describe separately labelled sign clips and per-class evaluation. Our interpretation is dynamic-sign classification, not a second qualifying CSLR study.

evidence.locator: Primary cited paper abstract reproduced on ResearchGate
evidence.passage: The mixed evaluation pools static and dynamic sign classes from an 80-sign dataset; it does not establish multi-sign continuous sequence recognition.

qualifying_studies: Takayama, Benitez-Garcia and Takahashi (2022), Skeleton-based online sign language recognition using monotonic attention
